analysis.investment_thesis: Aegis Logistics has a toll-road-like infrastructure business where operating profit has compounded at 21.9% for nine years even as reported revenues swung wildly with commodity prices — that is the mark of a quality underlying business. However, rapidly rising debt (borrowings up to 2,439 Cr, total debt 4,606 Cr in FY2025) and negative FCF from heavy terminal expansion keep me on the sidelines at current prices.
key_strengths: Promoter holding at 58.1% — meets my minimum; founders have real alignment with minority shareholders
Net profit compounding at 22.6% CAGR over 9 years with remarkable consistency despite revenue volatility — proof of a fee/throughput model insulated from commodity pricing swings
OCF positive in all 5 of the last 5 years; EBITDA grew from 208 Cr (2016) to 1,298 Cr (2025) — genuine value creation
key_risks: Finance costs have risen from 18 Cr (2016) to 165 Cr (2025), CAGR 27.9% — debt is growing faster than profits
Total debt of 4,606 Cr vs equity of 5,941 Cr implies a true leverage ratio closer to 0.77x, well above the reported 0.28 D/E; this discrepancy needs scrutiny
FCF has been negative in 3 of the last 5 years including -386 Cr in FY2025 as capex accelerates to 945 Cr — returns on new capital are yet to be proven
red_flags: Total debt of 4,606 Cr vs reported borrowings of 2,439 Cr — a 2,167 Cr unexplained gap (likely lease liabilities under IND-AS 116) that inflates true leverage
P/E of 32.4x is 60% above my preferred ceiling; investors are paying a premium that leaves no margin of safety
Investing cash outflows of 1,463 Cr in FY2025 represent nearly 2x operating cash flow — the company is growing through external financing, not internally generated surplus
analysis.detailed_analysis:
I find Aegis genuinely interesting as a business. The Liquid Terminal and Gas Terminal model is essentially infrastructure — clients need the terminals and switching costs are high once a supply chain is built around them. The fact that operating income grew steadily from 185 Cr (2016) to 1,098 Cr (2025) while revenues swung from 3,843 Cr to 8,627 Cr and back to 6,764 Cr tells you the business is fundamentally a throughput-fee model, not a commodity trader. That is exactly the predictability I look for. ROCE of 13.2% is below my 15% hurdle but trending in the right direction as new terminals ramp.

The problem is that Aegis is in a heavy expansion phase that requires significant external financing. Finance costs CAGR of 27.9% versus profit CAGR of 22.6% means debt is growing faster than earnings power. At 32.4x earnings, the market is already pricing in the successful ramp-up of all these new terminals. I would need to see debt stabilise, FCF turn consistently positive, and the price correct meaningfully — perhaps to 18-22x — before I would commit capital here. Good business, wrong price and balance sheet trajectory for today.
